paper_title: Dual Flow: Joint Image-Measurement Interpolation for Inverse Problems

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generative model-based approaches to linear inverse problems typically use the acquired noisy measurement to condition or guide sampling in the image domain. In this work, we introduce Dual Flow, a novel joint-flow model for solving linear inverse problems by jointly estimating the clean image and corresponding noise-free measurement from the observation. Specifically, Dual Flow formulates image reconstruction and measurement denoising as a coupled estimation problem, using coupled flows in the image and measurement domains. The acquired noisy measurement is used only to initialize the measurement state; thereafter, image and measurement states are jointly updated based on their current values. By construction, the final image and measurement estimates are guaranteed to satisfy the underlying forward model. We derive the sampling updates for the joint-flow which involves the conditional mean of the clean image given the joint state. We further derive a closed-form expression for a sufficient statistic of the joint state and show that the required conditional mean can be obtained by solving an image-domain Gaussian denoising problem involving operator-dependent, correlated noise. We train a velocity-prediction network using this formulation to estimate the conditional mean from the derived sufficient statistic. Extensive experiments across various linear inverse problems and image datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both distortion metrics and perceptual quality. Dual Flow requires no hyperparameter tuning beyond the number of inference steps and achieves shorter reconstruction times than competing methods. Additional analyses assess robustness to model mismatch, as well as the ability to generate diverse plausible reconstructions and characterize reconstruction uncertainty.

While the resulting optimization problems can often be efficiently solved using proximal splitting methods [8], [9], their reconstruction performance is often limited by the inability of hand-crafted regularizers to adequately capture complex image statistics. To overcome the limitations of hand-crafted regularizers, deep learning has emerged as powerful tool for developing datadriven image reconstruction methods. In plug-and-play (PnP) methods, the proximal operator, which can be interpreted as MAP denoiser under an assumed image prior, is replaced by learned denoiser, typically trained to minimize the mean squared error (MSE) [10][12]. Unrolled methods, on the other hand, convert fixed number of iterations of model-based reconstruction algorithm into trainable network, combining learned image updates with explicit data-consistency steps involve the forward operator. The learned parameters that are typically specialized to the imaging setting used during training [13][15]. Despite these advances, many existing reconstruction methods aim to produce single estimate of the unknown image from the given measurements, rather than generating diverse reconstructions that can enable the exploration of multiple plausible solutions and the characterization of reconstruction uncertainty, while potentially improving perceptual quality [16][18]. For instance, minimum mean-squared error (MMSE)-based reconstruction methods aim to approximate the posterior mean, which minimizes the expected squared reconstruction error but may lead to overly smooth images when the posterior distribution contains multiple distinct plausible solutions. MAPbased methods, on the other hand, seek to maximize the posterior density 𝑝(x1y0), yielding single reconstruction without capturing the uncertainty associated with the inverse problem. Generative models provide powerful framework for learning complex image distributions from data and generating diverse plausible samples. In particular, diffusion models and flow matching have emerged as effective approaches for modeling high-dimensional image distributions [19][21]. Diffusion models generate new samples by reversing gradual noisecorruption process, typically using learned score functions. learn timeFlow matching models, on the other hand, dependent velocity field that transports samples from simple source distribution to the target data distribution, often using straight-line interpolations between source and target samples during training [21], [22]. Both approaches can thus provide learned priors for image reconstruction. However, solving inverse problems requires incorporating the observed measurements into the generative process, rather than solely sampling from the learned image prior. major class of approaches for inverse problems addresses this by relying on pretrained unconditional generative models and incorporating measurement information only during inference. While these methods allow pretrained models to be reused across different inverse problems, accurately incorporating measurement information into the sampling process appears to be challenging. Many existing methods address this challenge through approximations of the likelihood score at intermediate stages to achieve posterior sampling [4], [23], [24], dataconsistency corrections applied to the sampling process of pretrained unconditional model [25][27], or Bayesian filtering techniques that employ weighted particles to approximate posterior sampling [28]. Despite their differences, these methods face limitations in posterior approximation accuracy and computational efficiency, as approximate measurementconditioning strategies can lead to deviations from the true posterior [29], while Bayesian filtering methods can improve posterior approximation accuracy at the expense of increased computational cost. While the aforementioned methods incorporate measurement information only during inference, an alternative class of approaches uses measurement information during training. For instance, conditional diffusion and flow matching methods train denoising or velocity-prediction networks using the acquired measurements or measurement-related quantities (such as Ay0) as conditioning inputs [30][32]. Once trained, these methods can generate measurement-conditioned reconstructions without separate correction steps during inference. However, conditioning on measurements alone does not guarantee consistency with the underlying forward model (i.e. physicsbased data consistency). Another line of work focuses on image restoration by learning deterministic or stochastic processes that progressively transform degraded observations into clean images [33][36]. More recently, posterior-score estimation has been reformulated as denoising problem involving operatordependent, correlated Gaussian noise, enabling learned denoiser to estimate the posterior score directly and perform posterior sampling without approximations and separate dataconsistency correction steps [37]. Existing generative model-based approaches to inverse problems typically use the acquired measurement y0 to condition or guide the sampling process in the image domain, rather than jointly modeling the image and the corresponding measurement. In this work, we introduce Dual Flow, novel joint flow model over the image and measurement domains for solving linear inverse problems, which enables the joint estimation of the unknown image and the corresponding noise-free measurement. Specifically, under the forward model in Eq. (1), we define joint imagemeasurement interpolation in which both the image and measurement states are defined through coupled straightline interpolations. In particular, the image state is interpolated between an initial random sample and the clean image x1, while the measurement state is interpolated between the acquired noisy measurement y0 and the noise-free measurement Ax1 of the final clean image. Thus, the two coupled flows evolve jointly, with the image-domain flow mapping the initial noise process to clean image estimate and the measurement-domain flow denoising the acquired measurement. These coupled interpolations provide the basis for learning joint flow dynamics in the image and measurement domains. In our development, we combine the image and measurement states into single variable, referred to as the joint state, and derive the sampling updates of this joint state for the reverse sampling procedure of Dual Flow. We show that these updates are governed by the conditional mean of the clean image random variable x1 given the current joint state. To this end, we derive (cid:101) closed-form sufficient statistic of the current joint state and show that estimating this conditional mean can be formulated as x1 denoising problem in which the clean image random variable (cid:101) is corrupted by operator-dependent correlated Gaussian noise. The derived sufficient statistic serves as the input to velocityprediction network, which is trained to obtain the conditional mean required for the joint-state sampling updates. We conduct comprehensive experiments across different linear inverse problems and image datasets, and compare the reconstruction quality, perceptual quality, and computational efficiency of Dual Flow against recent approaches. We also perform additional analyses to investigate the effect of the number of inference steps, robustness to varying degradation levels and model mismatch, and the ability to generate multiple plausible reconstructions and characterize reconstruction uncertainty. Numerical results demonstrate that Dual Flow achieves stateof-the-art performance, outperforming competing methods in terms of both distortion metrics and perceptual quality, while requiring substantially less reconstruction time and no additional hyperparameters beyond the number of inference steps. Visual comparisons further suggest that Dual Flow better avoids oversmoothing and artifacts while preserving fine textures and sharp details. Overall, these results demonstrate that Dual Flow achieves substantial improvements in perceptual quality without sacrificing distortion performance, yielding more favorable perceptiondistortion trade-off than competing methods. Unlike existing approaches that use the acquired noisy measurement y0 to guide the reconstruction of the unknown image, Dual Flow formulates linear inverse problems as joint estimation problem involving two coupled quantities: the clean image and its corresponding noise-free measurement. Specifically, it jointly addresses image reconstruction and measurement denoising within single reverse sampling procedure, while ensuring that the two estimates are related through the forward operator. Rather than repeatedly using the fixed noisy measurement y0 to guide the sampling process, Dual Flow uses it only to initialize the measurement state, with subsequent updates relying on the evolving joint state. To enable this joint sampling procedure, we derive closed-form expression for sufficient statistic of the current joint state, which serves as the input to the velocity-prediction network for estimating the conditional mean of the clean image. This exact formulation allows the network to fully incorporate the relevant image and measurement information without relying on hand-crafted measurement-related quantities or approximate measurement-conditioning strategies. Furthermore, Dual Flow requires no hyperparameter tuning beyond selecting the number of inference steps, whereas existing approaches often require multiple hyperparameters to be tuned for different inverse problems. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows: We develop Dual Flow, novel joint flow model for linear inverse problems that formulates image reconstruction and measurement denoising as coupled estimation problem. The proposed model jointly estimates the clean image and its corresponding noise-free measurement through coupled straight-line interpolations in the image and measurement domains, with the two estimates directly related by the underlying forward operator. We derive the sampling updates for the joint state and show that they are governed by the conditional mean of 3 the clean image given the current joint state. We further derive closed-form sufficient statistic of the joint state and show that estimating this conditional mean can be reformulated as denoising problem involving operatordependent, correlated Gaussian noise. Based on this reformulation, we develop velocityprediction network that takes the derived sufficient statistic as input to estimate the conditional mean required for joint state sampling. By using the acquired noisy measurement only to initialize the measurement state and relying on the evolving joint state for subsequent updates, Dual Flow avoids the need for hand-crafted measurementrelated conditioning inputs and approximate measurementconditioning strategies. Moreover, the proposed method does not require hyperparameter tuning beyond selecting the number of inference steps. We conduct comprehensive experiments across various linear inverse problems and image datasets, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in terms of both distortion metrics and perceptual quality, while requiring substantially less reconstruction time than competing methods. We also provide detailed analyses of the effects of the number of inference steps, robustness to varying degradation levels and model mismatch, reconstruction diversity, and uncertainty estimation. Section III presents the Dual Flow method in detail, including its mathematical formulation and relevant derivations. Section IV presents numerical results for various linear inverse problems, compares Dual Flow against recent methods, and provides detailed analyses of its performance. All images are normalized to [1, 1]. We use the standard training, validation, and test splits of CelebA. Since AFHQ-Cat does not have validation split, we reserve 32 images from its test set for validation. The acquired noisy measurements y0 are generated according to Eq. (1), with additive white Gaussian noise (0, 𝜎2I). We consider five linear inverse problems: denoising (𝜎 = 0.2); Gaussian deblurring with 61 61 kernel (𝜎𝑏 = 1 for CelebA and 𝜎𝑏 = 3 for AFHQ-Cat, where 𝜎𝑏 denotes the standard deviation of the blur kernel, and 𝜎 = 0.05); superresolution with 2 and 4 decimation for CelebA and AFHQCat, respectively (𝜎 = 0.05); random inpainting with 70% missing pixels (𝜎 = 0.01); and box inpainting with centered 40 40 and 80 80 missing regions for CelebA and AFHQ-Cat, respectively (𝜎 = 0.05). We evaluate each inverse problem on 100 test images per dataset. We compare the developed method with the recent flow-based algorithms PnP-Flow [26], Flower [27], OT-ODE [43], DFlow [44], and Flow-Priors [45], as well as the plug-and-play method PnP-GS [46] and the diffusion-based method PnPDiff [47]. For CelebA and AFHQ-Cat, all flow-based algorithms use the same pretrained, dataset-specific unconditional velocityprediction networks, while PnP-GS uses separately trained denoisers. Both the velocity-prediction networks and PnP-GS denoisers employ the same U-Net architecture [48], based on the implementations in [19], [49]. The velocity-prediction networks were trained using MiniBatch Optimal-Transport Flow Matching [38] with standard Gaussian latent distribution (0, I). Training was performed using the Adam optimizer with learning rate of 104 for 200 and 400 epochs on CelebA and AFHQ-Cat, respectively, with corresponding batch sizes of 128 and 64. For PnP-Diff, following PnP-Flow [26], we use pretrained diffusion model from [50], trained on the FFHQ dataset [51], since training diffusion model with the same U-Net yielded poor results due to insufficient model capacity. Conclusion In this paper, we developed Dual Flow, novel joint flow model for solving linear inverse problems by jointly estimating the clean image and its corresponding noise-free measurement. The key idea is to jointly evolve the image and measurement states, rather than repeatedly using the acquired noisy measurement to condition or guide the reverse sampling process. This formulation enables image reconstruction and measurement denoising to be addressed as two coupled estimation tasks within single sampling procedure. Our method does not require approximate measurement-conditioning strategies or any additional hyperparameters beyond the number of inference steps. By construction, the final image and measurement estimates are guaranteed to satisfy the forward model. Extensive experiments across five linear inverse problems on two image datasets demonstrate that Dual Flow achieves stateof-the-art performance in both distortion metrics and perceptual quality, while requiring substantially less reconstruction time than competing methods. Visually, Dual Flow better preserves fine textures and sharp details while reducing over-smoothing and reconstruction artifacts. These findings demonstrate more favorable perceptiondistortion trade-off than competing methods. Moreover, we showed that Dual Flow can generate diverse plausible reconstructions, enabling uncertainty estimation. Despite its strong reconstruction performance, Dual Flow remains sensitive to forward-operator mismatch between training and testing. Reconstruction Diversity and Uncertainty Estimation Beyond reconstruction accuracy, we investigate the reconstruction diversity and uncertainty estimation capabilities of Dual Flow-W. Point estimators, such as MAP or MMSE estimators, provide single reconstruction. Although such estimates can be optimal under their respective estimation criteria, single reconstruction cannot capture the full range of plausible solutions, thereby discarding information about uncertainty and reconstruction diversity. Dual Flow-W addresses this limitation by generating 𝐾 reconstructions for the same acquired noisy measurement through joint-state sampling, starting from 𝐾 independent initial samples x(0) 𝑗 (0, I), 𝑗 = 1, . . . , 𝐾. These reconstructions represent different plausible solutions supported by the learned joint flow model rather than random perturbations of single estimate. The samples tend to agree in regions strongly constrained by the measurements, whereas regions with limited information due to the forward operator, noise, or missing observations may exhibit greater variability. This enables pixelwise uncertainty estimation directly from the generated reconstructions. Fig. 5 of the main paper demonstrates three representative reconstructions and the predicted uncertainty map computed from the 𝐾 = 6 samples generated by Dual Flow-W for representative box-inpainting example from CelebA. The sample reconstructions exhibit variations in the missing region. These variations are particularly noticeable in fine facial details, such as the eyebrow, where the uncertainty map also exhibits higher standard deviations. These results illustrate that Dual Flow-W provides diverse plausible reconstructions and uncertainty estimates as an intrinsic byproduct of its sampling procedure, without requiring additional network evaluations beyond those used to generate the reconstruction samples. Numerical Results on AFHQ-Cat We evaluate the compared methods on AFHQ-Cat dataset over 100 test images. Table presents the corresponding quantitative results. Dual Flow-W achieves the highest PSNR for all five inverse problems except random inpainting, while obtaining the best or near-best SSIM across all five problems. Dual Flow-T achieves the lowest LPIPS across all five problems. Similar to the results on CelebA, Dual Flow requires substantially less reconstruction time than all competing methods, except PnP-GS for denoising. The qualitative results in Figs. 8 and 9 show that Dual Flow-T preserves fine textures and sharp details while introducing fewer artifacts and avoiding the oversmoothing observed in competing methods. These results further demonstrate that Dual Flow-T provides better balance between perceptual quality and distortion performance compared with competing methods.
